# CI workflows

Read this before editing anything under `.github/`. Dependency PRs themselves are in
[dependencies.md](../docs/guidelines/dependencies.md).

**Dependabot PRs merge themselves from the last job in `ci.yml`, and every guard there is load-bearing.** `dependabot-auto-merge` approves and squash-merges once every other CI job has passed on the same commit. It replaced a `workflow_run` workflow that interpolated `head_branch` into a shell (injection) while holding a write token. The workflow rules below are pinned by `test/integration/ci_workflow_test.rb`; the repository settings in the last bullet are not, so check them by hand when the job stops merging:

- **Trust the PR, never `github.actor`.** The actor can be made `dependabot[bot]` on someone else's PR ("Dependabot confusion"). The job checks the PR author, that the head branch lives in this repository, and that every commit is authored by Dependabot and signature-verified. GitHub lists at most 250 of a PR's commits, so a longer PR is left for review too. A human commit pushed onto a Dependabot branch therefore leaves the PR for review, while a maintainer re-running CI or reopening the PR still gets it merged.
- **Approve and merge only the head CI tested.** The approval is pinned with `commit_id` and the merge with `--match-head-commit`, so a push that lands after CI passed is never approved or merged unseen. `gh pr review --approve` approves whatever the head is at that moment, which is why the job calls the reviews API instead. CI ran against the head merged with main *as it was then*; main does not require branches to be up to date, so the squash can land on a newer main. Same trade-off a human merge makes.
- **`needs:` lists every CI job.** A job missing from it is a check Dependabot PRs merge without.
- **No `${{ }}` inside `run:`**, in any workflow. Pass values through `env:` and quote `"$VAR"`.
- **No `workflow_run`, `pull_request_target` or `issue_comment` triggers.** They can run with write access on untrusted input. On `pull_request` a fork, and Dependabot, normally gets a read-only token whatever the workflow requests, but a repository or organization setting ("Send write tokens to workflows from pull requests") can change that, so never rely on the event type alone: grant least-privilege `permissions:` and check where the head lives, as the auto-merge job does.
- **The repo must let workflows approve PRs** (Settings → Actions → "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests"). Main's one required review is satisfied by that approval. Turning on "Require review from Code Owners" with a CODEOWNERS file would block it: a workflow's approval is not a code owner's. Keep "Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed" on, so the pinned approval can't satisfy the review on a later head. Set the default workflow token to read-only; `ci.yml` grants write only to this job.
- **Every job runs on Blacksmith** (`blacksmith-<n>vcpu-ubuntu-2404`; the org's Blacksmith app must include this repository, or jobs queue forever). `actions/cache` and `setup-ruby`'s bundler cache use Blacksmith's cache with no changes. Caches saved on GitHub's runners don't carry over, so the first run after the move was cold. Size a job by what it parallelises: the unit tests run one worker per core on 8 vCPUs.
- **The system tests run as one job: ten workers on 32 vCPUs.** Each worker runs its own Chrome, and a Chrome short of cores drops clicks, so keep about three vCPUs per worker when changing either number. On 26 Oct 2026 this matched twelve 4-vCPU jobs split by test ([PR #629](https://github.com/mr-yum/growth-os/pull/629)): 190s against 187s for the slowest shard. Each shard spent about 65s on setup before testing, and Rails' worker queue balances load better than fixed shards. 32 vCPUs is Blacksmith's largest Linux runner; if the suite outgrows it, split it across jobs by test, not by file (two files hold a fifth of the suite). Its commits have a working version.
- **The feedback exchange's Pact checks are split across two workflows.** `ci.yml`'s `contract` job (in `needs:` like every other) runs the consumer tests, fails if `contract/pacts/growthos-chip.json` is not what they write, and verifies the branch against Chip's deployed pact. `contract.yml` holds the `contract-change` label gate, which must re-run when a label changes (so it cannot sit in `ci.yml` without re-running everything), and the nightly re-verification. Both peers' `/contract` addresses are repository variables (`FEEDBACK_EXCHANGE_PEER_CONTRACT_URL`, `FEEDBACK_EXCHANGE_OWN_CONTRACT_URL`), never literals; while one is unset its check passes with a warning. See [feedback-exchange.md → Contract tests](../docs/guidelines/feedback-exchange.md#contract-tests-pact).
